controversies/territorial-spirits-debate: Should Christians identify and pray against demonic powers ruling cities and nations, or is that unbiblical speculation?
Strategic-level spiritual warfare and territorial spirits

From the late 1980s C. Peter Wagner and others promoted “strategic-level spiritual warfare” against territorial spirits, citing Daniel 10 and the Argentine revival; evangelical scholars and the Lausanne movement warned against speculation and animistic tendencies. The debate continues in disputes over the New Apostolic Reformation.

Scripture shows angelic princes over nations (Daniel 10) and Paul says we wrestle not against flesh and blood but against principalities. Where intercessors have identified strongholds, repented for a city’s sins and prayed with authority, as in Argentina, the gospel has broken through. To ignore the unseen battle is to fight with one hand tied.
No apostolic example of mapping or naming territorial spirits

The devil is real and defeated. The New Testament calls believers to resist him by faith, holiness and the proclamation of the gospel, never to map or address territorial spirits. Seeking hidden knowledge about demons comes close to the animism the gospel dethrones, and distracts from repentance, discipleship and social witness.
Ephesians 6:13-18 (the armour is defensive and gospel-centred)

Both sides miss the social face of the powers. The principalities are embodied in empires, economies and institutions; Christ’s cross unmasks them, and the church engages them through truth-telling and nonviolent resistance rather than prayer techniques alone.
Reduces personal demons to social forces
Carlos Annacondia’s campaigns in Argentina feature mass deliverance.
Wagner and the AD2000 United Prayer Track promote territorial-spirit prayer.
Engaging the Enemy (ed. Wagner); George Otis Jr. popularises “spiritual mapping”.
Lausanne statement on spiritual warfare warns against excesses.
Chuck Lowe’s Territorial Spirits and World Evangelisation? published by OMF.
Wagner proclaims a “Second Apostolic Age”; NAR networks expand.

Unresolved. Strategic-level warfare remains influential in NAR and many neo-charismatic networks worldwide, while most evangelical scholars, cessationists and many Pentecostals regard it as speculative.
Shaped global prayer movements and NAR political engagement.
Provoked a large evangelical literature on spiritual warfare.
Raised missiological questions about animism and contextualisation.
controversies/witch-hunts-and-demonology: How did Christian demonology contribute to the early modern witch-hunts, and what ended them?

Between about 1450 and 1750, Catholic and Protestant courts executed tens of thousands of people, mostly women, for witchcraft understood as a pact with the devil. Christian sceptics — Weyer, Spee, Salazar, Bekker, Increase Mather — challenged the trials, and today all churches repudiate them. The episode remains a test case for the dangers of demonology.

As they saw it, Scripture commands that a witch shall not live; Satan seeks to destroy Christendom through a secret sect bound to him by pact; confessions and the testimony of the afflicted proved the crime; and to doubt witchcraft was to doubt Scripture and the reality of the devil. Rulers who failed to prosecute endangered their people.
Spectral evidence can be the devil impersonating the innocent

The devil is a liar, so testimony shaped by him — spectral evidence — is worthless; torture makes anyone confess; God, not Satan, governs nature; and Christ commands justice and mercy. Better that the guilty escape than the innocent be condemned.
Salazar’s investigation in the Basque country (1611)
Accused by contemporaries of denying Scripture or the devil
Johann Weyer’s De praestigiis daemonum argues accused witches are deluded or ill.
Inquisitor Alonso de Salazar Frías finds no evidence in the Basque trials; the Spanish Inquisition effectively halts executions.
Anna Göldi, among the last executed for witchcraft in Europe, in Glarus, Switzerland.

Witch prosecutions declined from the late 17th century through judicial scepticism, legal reform, theological critique and changing world-views, and ended in Europe by the late 18th century. All major churches now repudiate them. However, witchcraft accusations — sometimes fuelled by church leaders, sometimes opposed by them — persist in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, India and Papua New Guinea.
Became a lasting indictment of religious persecution and misogyny.
Contributed to Enlightenment scepticism about the devil and to legal reforms against torture.
Informs contemporary church efforts against witchcraft accusations in Africa and the Pacific.
controversies/penal-substitution-vs-chri: Is the heart of the atonement Christ bearing the penalty of God’s justice in our place, or God’s victory in Christ over sin, death and the powers?

A 20th- and 21st-century debate sharpened by Aulén’s Christus Victor (1930) and by evangelical controversies (Chalke 2003; Pierced for Our Transgressions 2007), over which model is central and whether they can be combined.

Our deepest problem is guilt before a holy God. The good news is that God himself, in the Son, took our place under judgement and bore the curse. Only so is forgiveness both free and just, and only so can the troubled conscience rest. Victory over the powers is real — but the devil’s weapon is accusation, which is disarmed when our guilt is removed.
Risk of pitting Father against Son.

From the fathers to Luther, the church sang of the cross as God’s triumph. Our plight is bondage — to sin, death and the devil — and God himself comes to set us free. The resurrection is no mere sequel but the victory itself. To make the Father’s wrath the main problem is to shrink the gospel and distort God’s face.
Anselm’s Cur Deus Homo moves the West toward satisfaction.
Calvin’s Institutes II.16 sets out penal substitution.
Steve Chalke’s Lost Message of Jesus sparks controversy in the UK Evangelical Alliance.
Pierced for Our Transgressions defends penal substitution.

No council has ever defined a single theory. Confessional Reformed and many evangelical bodies treat penal substitution as essential; Orthodox, many Anabaptist and some mainline theologians prefer Christus Victor. A widespread contemporary view (the "kaleidoscopic" approach) sees the models as complementary, though which is central remains disputed.
Divides evangelical institutions and fuels "progressive" vs conservative identity debates.
controversies/anselm-vs-abelard/question: Is the cross directed chiefly toward God (satisfying his justice or honour) or toward us (revealing love that transforms)?
controversies/anselm-vs-abelard/title: Satisfaction vs moral influence (Anselm and Abelard)
controversies/anselm-vs-abelard/summary: The medieval contrast between "objective" and "subjective" atonement, crystallised by Anselm (1098) and Abelard (c.1135), and repeated in the Reformation, Socinian and liberal debates.
controversies/anselm-vs-abelard/sides/0/: Sin is not merely a bad example; it is a real disorder in the relation between creature and Creator. God in mercy provides what we cannot: a God-man who freely restores the honour owed. Without something objective done for us, love would be only a spectacle.
Death isolated from life and resurrection.
controversies/anselm-vs-abelard/sides/1/: God needed no price to forgive. The barrier is our hard hearts. In Christ, God loves us to the end, and that love wins us back. Redemption is the love that the cross kindles in us.
controversies/anselm-vs-abelard/timeline: Bernard of Clairvaux’s letter against Abelard’s errors.
Council of Sens condemns propositions of Abelard.
Hastings Rashdall’s The Idea of Atonement defends Abelard.
controversies/anselm-vs-abelard/resoluti: Abelard was condemned and satisfaction became the Western norm, but the "subjective" dimension was absorbed by Aquinas and later theologians, revived by liberal Protestantism, and is now generally treated as one true aspect of the atonement rather than a complete account.
controversies/anselm-vs-abelard/conseque: The objective/subjective framework became the standard typology of atonement theories.
controversies/extent-of-the-atonement/qu: Did Christ die to secure the salvation of the elect only, or to make salvation possible for all?
controversies/extent-of-the-atonement/ti: For whom did Christ die? (Extent of the atonement)
controversies/extent-of-the-atonement/su: A Protestant debate from Gottschalk’s precedent through Dort (1619), Owen (1647), Amyraut and Wesley to the present, over "limited" (definite) versus "unlimited" (general) atonement.
controversies/extent-of-the-atonement/si: Christ did not die to make salvation merely possible but to save. The Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. If he bore the punishment of every sin of every person, none could justly be condemned. His death is infinitely sufficient for all, but God designed it to be effectual for his people.
Unity of the Trinity’s saving purpose.

Christ is "the propitiation … for the sins of the whole world" and "gave himself a ransom for all". Unless Christ died for every hearer, the gospel cannot be offered sincerely to every hearer. The atonement is universal in provision and becomes effectual through faith.
controversies/extent-of-the-atonement/ti: Gottschalk condemned at Quierzy for teaching that Christ died only for the elect.
Canons of Dort, Second Head: sufficient for all, efficient for the elect.
Owen’s The Death of Death in the Death of Christ.
Wesley’s sermon "Free Grace" opens the Calvinist-Methodist rift with Whitefield.
controversies/extent-of-the-atonement/re: Reformed confessions teach definite atonement (though hypothetical universalism was tolerated at Dort and Westminster); Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist, Arminian Baptist and Pentecostal churches teach that Christ died for all. Barth reframed the question through election in Christ.
controversies/extent-of-the-atonement/co: Shapes how evangelists phrase the gospel offer ("Christ died for you").
